questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: History: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
questions.text:
Match the following attributes of allegory of Germania with its significance :
a. Broken Chains
b. Breast-Plate with eagle
c. Crown of oak leaves
d. Sword
I. Heroism II. Readiness to fight III. Strength IV. Being free
questions.solution: Broken chains: being freed; breastplate with eagle: symbol of the German empire, strength; crown of oak leaves: heroism; sword: readiness to fight.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: History: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.text: Which one of the following aspects was common between the writings of B.R. Ambedkar and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker ?
options: Wrote on the caste system in India
Motivated Indians for their national freedom.
questions.solution: Both wrote powerfully against the caste system and caste discrimination.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Who of the following set up the first Iron and Steel industry in India ?
questions.solution: The Tatas set up the first iron and steel plant in India at Jamshedpur (1912), as the textbook puts it. (It was founded by J.N. Tata's company; of the options given, the Tata name is the intended answer.)

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.text:
Arrange the following in chronological order :
I. The Bretton Woods conference established the International Monetary Fund.
II. The Second World War broke out between the Axis and Allied groups.
III. A car manufacturer Henry Ford adopted the 'Assembly Line Method' for production.
IV. The Western economies organized themselves as a group – 'The Group of 77'.
questions.solution: Ford's assembly line (1913), the Second World War (1939), Bretton Woods (1944), and the G-77 (1964). (Note: the G-77 was in fact formed by developing countries, not Western economies.)

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Identify the crop : • This is the second most important Cereal Crop. • This is a Rabi crop. • It requires a cool growing season and bright sunshine at the time of ripening. • It requires 50 to 75 cm annual rainfall.
questions.solution: Wheat is India's second most important cereal, a rabi crop that needs a cool growing season, bright sunshine at ripening and 50–75 cm of rain.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: In which of the following States Tungabhadra Dam is located ?
questions.solution: The Tungabhadra Dam is at Hosapete in Karnataka.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which of the following pair is correctly matched ?
questions.solution: Alluvial soil covers the northern plains of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. Black soil is in the Deccan, arid soil in Rajasthan and laterite soil in hot, rainy areas.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which of the following countries has the highest 'Life Expectancy' at the birth ?
questions.solution: In the textbook's Human Development table, Bangladesh has the highest life expectancy at birth (about 72.6 years) of these four countries.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.text: Which one of the following organization is providing data regarding employment in India ?
questions.solution: Employment data in India is collected and published by the National Statistical Office (NSO).

questions.chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.text: Which one of the following pair is correctly matched ?
questions.solution: Fishing uses a natural resource directly, so fishermen are in the primary sector. A priest is tertiary and a basket weaver secondary.

questions.text: Assume there are four families in a locality. If the monthly income of each family is ₹10,000, ₹20,000, ₹30,000 and ₹40,000, then what is the average income of the locality ?

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.text: Kanta works in an office. She gets her salary regularly at the end of every month. In addition to the salary, she also gets other benefits laid down by the government. In which of the following sector Kanta is working ?
questions.solution: Regular salary and benefits under government rules are features of the organised sector.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which one of the following is a formal source of credit ?
questions.solution: Banks and cooperatives are formal sources; relatives, traders and moneylenders are informal.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Consider the following statements on Power Sharing :
I. It deepens democracy.
II. It helps to reduce conflicts among social groups.
III. It is a way to ensure political stability.
IV. It brings socio-economic struggles.
questions.solution: Power sharing deepens democracy, reduces conflict between social groups and ensures political stability. It does not bring socio-economic struggles.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Match Column A (Subjects) with Column B (List) :
I. Defence II. Police III. Marriage IV. Computer Software
1. Concurrent List 2. Union List 3. State List 4. Residuary Subjects
questions.solution: Defence is in the Union List, police in the State List, marriage in the Concurrent List, and computer software is a residuary subject.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Which one of the following is the most popular form of government in the contemporary world ?
questions.solution: Democracy is the most widely accepted and popular form of government today.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Political Science: Gender, Religion and Caste
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Women in different parts of the World organized themselves and agitated for equal rights.
Reason (R): Women's movement aimed at equality in personal and family life as well.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution: Women organised to demand voting rights, better education and careers, and more radical movements also sought equality in personal and family life. Both are true, but R describes a further aim rather than explaining why women organised.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Political Science: Gender, Religion and Caste
questions.text: Which one of the following matters do NOT deal with the 'Family Laws' ?
questions.solution: Family laws deal with marriage, divorce, adoption and inheritance, not finance.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: History: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
questions.text: Explain Romanticism as a cultural movement in Europe.
questions.solution: Romanticism was a cultural movement that sought to develop a particular form of nationalist sentiment. Romantic artists and poets criticised the glorification of reason and science and focused on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings. They tried to create a sense of shared collective heritage and a common cultural past through folk songs, folk poetry, folk dances and vernacular language, as Herder did in Germany.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: History: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
questions.text: Explain Frederic Sorrieu's dream in the context of democratic and social republics in France during 1848.
questions.solution: In 1848 the French artist Frederic Sorrieu prepared a series of four prints visualising his dream of a world made up of 'democratic and social republics'. The first print shows the peoples of Europe and America, of all ages and social classes, marching in a long train and paying homage to the Statue of Liberty, holding the Declaration of the Rights of Man. On the ground lie the shattered remains of the symbols of absolutist institutions. Each nation is identified by its flag and national costume.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Mention any two features of Plantation agriculture.
questions.solution: Any two: a single crop is grown on a large area; it uses a lot of capital and migrant labour; the produce is mainly used as raw material in industries; it depends on a well-developed network of transport and communication, processing industries and markets. Examples: tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Political Science: Gender, Religion and Caste
questions.text: Explain any two provisions that make India a secular state.
questions.solution: Any two: there is no official religion for the Indian state; the Constitution gives all individuals and communities freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion; it prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion; it allows the state to intervene in religious matters to ensure equality within religious communities.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.text: Imagine that you are the village Head. Suggest any two activities that you think should be taken up to increase the income of the villagers.
questions.solution: Any two: build irrigation facilities (wells, check dams) so farmers can grow more than one crop; set up small-scale and cottage industries such as dal mills, food processing or handicrafts; arrange cheap credit through banks and cooperatives; build roads and storage so produce can reach markets; promote animal husbandry, poultry, fishing or tourism; make use of MGNREGA work for village assets.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: History: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.text: Explain the implication of print culture on the religious reforms in India during 19th century.
questions.solution: From the early 19th century there were intense debates on religious issues. Print let reformers such as Raja Ram Mohun Roy (through the Sambad Kaumudi) criticise practices like widow immolation and idolatry, while orthodox Hindus answered through papers such as the Samachar Chandrika. Printed tracts and newspapers spread new ideas and shaped the debate among ordinary people. Muslim ulama (for example the Deoband Seminary) published thousands of fatwas, and cheap religious texts in vernacular languages, such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, reached many people. Print connected communities across India and encouraged public discussion of religion.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: How has Information Technology affected Electronic Industry ? Explain.
questions.solution: The electronics industry covers products from transistor sets to televisions, telephones, computers and other equipment. Bengaluru has become the electronic capital of India, along with centres such as Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and Kolkata, and many software technology parks provide single-window services and high-speed data communication. The IT and electronics industry has created a great deal of employment and is a major earner of foreign exchange through business process outsourcing (BPO) and software exports.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: 'The question of sustainability of development raises many fundamentally new issues about the nature and process of development.' Explain it with examples.
questions.solution: Development that uses resources faster than they can be renewed cannot last. Groundwater is renewable, but overuse in parts of India is lowering water tables; crude oil and minerals are non-renewable and will run out. The consequences of environmental damage, such as pollution and climate change, do not respect national or state borders. So development must meet present needs without compromising future generations, which raises new questions about how development should be planned and measured.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Explain any three functions of Political Party.
questions.solution: Any three: parties contest elections; they put forward policies and programmes for voters to choose from; they play a decisive role in making laws; they form and run governments; parties that lose play the role of opposition; they shape public opinion; they give people access to government machinery and welfare schemes.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Explain any three functions of the Reserve Bank of India.
questions.solution: The RBI issues currency notes on behalf of the central government. It supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans: banks must keep a minimum cash balance out of deposits, and the RBI checks that this is maintained. It sees that banks give loans not just to profit-making businesses but also to small cultivators, small industries and small borrowers, and banks must report to it how much they lend, to whom and at what interest rate.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Explain the role of banks with regard to money which they accept from the public.
questions.solution: Banks keep only a small part (about 15%) of the deposits as cash to meet withdrawals. They use the major portion to give loans to people and businesses, so banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (depositors) and those who need funds (borrowers). Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits; the difference is their main source of income. Deposits also earn interest and can be withdrawn on demand or used through cheques.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Analyse the implications of First World War on the economic and Political situation of India.
questions.solution: Economic: defence spending rose hugely, financed by war loans and higher taxes; customs duties were raised and income tax introduced; prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, causing great hardship; crops failed in 1918–19 and 1920–21, leading to food shortages, and an influenza epidemic killed 12–13 million people. Political: forced recruitment of soldiers in villages caused widespread anger; people hoped their hardships would end after the war, but the Rowlatt Act followed. This created a new political situation in which Gandhiji launched mass movements and nationalism spread to new groups.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Analyse the role of folklore and symbols in the revival of nationalism in India during late 19th century.
questions.solution: Nationalists recorded folk tales sung by bards and toured villages to gather folk songs and legends, believing they gave a true picture of traditional culture damaged by outside forces; Rabindranath Tagore in Bengal and Natesa Sastri in Madras led this work. The image of Bharat Mata was created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (Vande Mataram) and painted by Abanindranath Tagore, giving the nation a visual identity. During the Swadeshi movement a tricolour flag (red, green and yellow) was designed, and Gandhiji's flag of 1921 had the spinning wheel at its centre. Reinterpreting history to show India's past glory also gave Indians pride and a sense of collective belonging.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: 'Efficient means of Transport are pre-requisite for fast development.' Justify the statement.
questions.solution: Transport carries raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets, so production and trade depend on it. It links producers and consumers, widens markets and supports national and international trade. It helps agriculture by carrying inputs and produce, and lets people travel for work, education and services. It supports defence, administration and disaster relief, and connects remote and backward areas, reducing regional imbalance. Dense, efficient transport networks are therefore a prerequisite for fast development.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: 'Roadways have an edge over Railways.' Justify the statement.
questions.solution: Construction cost of roads is much lower than railway lines. Roads can cross more uneven and dissected terrain and reach mountains such as the Himalayas. Road transport is economical for small numbers of people and small amounts of goods over short distances. It provides door-to-door service, which lowers loading and unloading costs. Roads also act as a feeder to other modes, linking railway stations, ports and airports.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: "There is an overwhelming support for the idea of democracy all over the world." Support the statement with examples.
questions.solution: More than a hundred countries now claim to practise some form of democratic politics, with formal constitutions, elections and political parties. Even people who complain about their governments support the idea of democracy and want their own rule. Surveys in South Asia, for example, show strong support for democracy across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. Democratic governments are accountable, responsive and legitimate; they promote equality and dignity; and they allow peaceful resolution of conflicts and correction of mistakes, which is why people prefer them.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: "Democracy can address all socio-economic and political problems." Support the statement with arguments.
questions.solution: Democracy cannot solve every problem instantly, but it is better able to address them than other systems. It produces an accountable and responsive government, chosen by the people, that must listen to their needs. Through debate and consultation it improves the quality of decisions. It accommodates social diversity and lets conflicts be resolved peacefully. It promotes equality, dignity and freedom, and as people get rights they can press for economic and social justice. Mistakes can be corrected through elections and public criticism.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.text: Analyse the impact of globalization in India.
questions.solution: Positive: consumers, especially well-off urban people, have more choice and better quality at lower prices; MNCs have increased investment and created new jobs; local companies supplying MNCs have prospered; some Indian companies such as Tata Motors and Infosys have become MNCs themselves; services such as IT have grown. Negative: small producers and manufacturers (for example batteries, plastics, toys) have faced severe competition and many units shut down; workers increasingly face insecure, flexible employment with low wages and fewer benefits. The benefits have not been shared equally.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.text: Analyse the ways to make globalization fair.
questions.solution: The government should ensure labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights; support small producers to improve their performance until they become strong enough to compete; use trade and investment barriers where needed to protect domestic interests; negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules; and align with other developing countries to fight against the domination of developed countries. People's organisations and campaigns can also influence decisions on trade and investment.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Market for Goods: One way in which new consumers are created is through advertisements. As you know, advertisements make products appear desirable and necessary. They try to shape the minds of people and create new needs. Today we live in a world where advertisements surround us. They appear in newspapers, magazines, hoardings, street walls, television screens. But if we look back into history, we find that from the very beginning of the industrial age, advertisements have played a part in expanding the markets for products, and in shaping a new consumer culture. When Manchester industrialists began selling cloth in India, they put labels on the cloth bundles. The label was needed to make the place of manufacture and the name of the company familiar to the buyer. The label was also to be a mark of quality. When buyers saw 'MADE IN MANCHESTER' written in bold on the label, they were expected to feel confident about buying the cloth.

How was the marketing of goods done in India by the British ?
questions.solution: Through labels on the cloth bundles (such as 'MADE IN MANCHESTER') and later through images, calendars and advertisements that made the goods familiar and appealing.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Market for Goods: One way in which new consumers are created is through advertisements. Advertisements make products appear desirable and necessary. They try to shape the minds of people and create new needs.

How were the new consumers created through advertisement during colonial India ?
questions.solution: Advertisements made products look desirable and necessary and created new needs, using familiar images of gods, goddesses and important figures so people trusted and wanted the goods.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Market for Goods: From the very beginning of the industrial age, advertisements have played a part in expanding the markets for products, and in shaping a new consumer culture. When Manchester industrialists began selling cloth in India, they put labels on the cloth bundles. The label was needed to make the place of manufacture and the name of the company familiar to the buyer. The label was also to be a mark of quality.

Identify the messages conveyed through advertisements during industrialization.
questions.solution: Labels made the place of manufacture and company name familiar and acted as a mark of quality. Images of Indian gods and goddesses gave the goods divine approval and made them seem familiar. Calendars hung in homes and shops spread the message all year. Later, Indian manufacturers' advertisements carried the nationalist message: if you care for the nation, buy products made by Indians (Swadeshi).

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Conservation of Energy Resources: Energy is a basic requirement for economic development. Every sector of the national economy – agriculture, industry, transport, commercial and domestic – needs inputs of energy. The economic development plans implemented since independence necessarily required increasing amounts of energy to remain operational. As a result, consumption of energy in all forms has been steadily rising all over the country. In this background, there is an urgent need to develop a sustainable path of energy development. Promotion of energy conservation and increased use of renewable energy sources are the twin planks of sustainable energy. India is presently one of the least energy efficient countries in the world. We have to adopt a cautious approach for the judicious use of our limited energy resources. For example, as concerned citizens we can do our bit by using public transport systems instead of individual vehicles; switching off electricity when not in use, using power-saving devices and using non-conventional sources of energy. At last "Energy Saved is energy produced".

Why is sustainable energy a key to sustainable development ?
questions.solution: Every sector of the economy needs energy, and fossil fuels are limited, so development can continue into the future only if energy is used efficiently and comes increasingly from renewable sources.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Conservation of Energy Resources: Every sector of the national economy – agriculture, industry, transport, commercial and domestic – needs inputs of energy. The economic development plans implemented since independence necessarily required increasing amounts of energy to remain operational.

Why is consumption of energy rising in all over India ?
questions.solution: Development plans since independence have expanded agriculture, industry, transport and domestic use, all of which need more and more energy.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Conservation of Energy Resources: As concerned citizens we can do our bit by using public transport systems instead of individual vehicles; switching off electricity when not in use, using power-saving devices and using non-conventional sources of energy. At last "Energy Saved is energy produced".

Explain 'Energy saved is energy produced'.
questions.solution: Every unit of energy saved means one unit less has to be generated from scarce resources such as coal and oil, so saving energy has the same effect as producing it. It also reduces costs and pollution. We can save energy by using public transport, switching off lights and appliances when not needed, and using power-saving devices.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Decentralisation in India: When power is taken away from Central and State governments and given to local government, it is called decentralization. The basic idea behind decentralization is that there are a large number of problems and issues which are best settled at the local level. People have better knowledge of problems in their localities. They also have better ideas on where to spend money and how to manage things more efficiently. Besides, at the local level it is possible for the people to directly participate in decision making. This helps to inculcate a habit of democratic participation. Local government is the best way to realise one important principle of democracy, namely local self-government. The need for decentralisation was recognized in our Constitution. Since then, there have been several attempts to decentralize power to the level of villages and towns. Panchayats in villages and municipalities in urban areas were set up in all the States. But these were directly under the control of State Governments. Elections to these local governments were not held regularly.

Explain Decentralization in democracy.
questions.solution: Decentralisation means taking power away from the central and state governments and giving it to local governments, so local problems can be settled locally.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Decentralisation in India: At the local level it is possible for the people to directly participate in decision making. This helps to inculcate a habit of democratic participation. Local government is the best way to realise one important principle of democracy, namely local self-government.

Explain the importance of Local self Government in democracy.
questions.solution: It lets people participate directly in decisions about their area, uses their local knowledge to solve problems efficiently, and builds a habit of democratic participation.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Decentralisation in India: The need for decentralisation was recognized in our Constitution. Since then, there have been several attempts to decentralize power to the level of villages and towns.

Describe any two steps taken by Indian government for decentralization.
questions.solution: Any two from the 1992 constitutional amendment: regular elections to local bodies made compulsory; seats reserved for SCs, STs and OBCs, and at least one-third for women; State Election Commissions set up to conduct local elections; state governments required to share some powers and revenue with local bodies.
